title: Northpeak AI - technical deep dive: tail latency under mixed short/long prompts
summary: Northpeak described user-visible p95 latency spikes when short chat requests are interleaved with long-context / RAG-heavy prompts (mixed workload). Current symptoms look like head-of-line blocking during prefill and unstable batching decisions. Redwood shared an in-flight scheduler prototype (short/long classification + two-queue dispatch with aging + per-iteration token budgets) aimed at reducing p95 without major throughput regression. Northpeak success criteria: materially improve p95/TTFT for short prompts under mixed load while guaranteeing progress for long prompts and keeping cost/throughput within bounds. Team agreed to run a joint benchmark using Redwood’s mixed-workload scenarios (80/20, 50/50, long-spike) and, if possible, replay a sanitized slice of Northpeak traces.
topics: Context + current stack; Tail latency symptoms (TTFT vs decode p95); Mixed workload distributions (short chat vs long-context); Prefill vs decode contention; Continuous batching and KV cache interactions; Redwood short/long prompt-aware scheduling prototype; Fairness/starvation guardrails (aging, max skew, burst caps); Benchmark plan + success metrics; Deployment options (Hosted vs Dedicated/VPC) + security constraints; Next steps and owners
questions: What is Northpeak’s current p95/p99 SLO for TTFT and end-to-end latency?; What is the prompt/context length distribution (p50/p95 tokens, long tail)?; Are spikes correlated with prefill time, queue time, or decode time?; What GPU SKU/region constraints matter (H100 vs A100, multi-region)?; What fairness guarantees are required for long-context jobs (max wait, max slowdown)?; Can Northpeak provide anonymized/synthetic trace stats (no content) to tune short/long thresholds?
next_steps: Redwood to share benchmark input format + mixed workload scenarios list (80/20, 50/50, long-spike) and required metrics (TTFT, queue time, p95/p99, throughput).
Northpeak to send prompt-length distribution stats (bucketed) and concurrency profile (QPS and burstiness) by Friday.
Redwood to run benchmark on two SKUs (A100 80GB and H100) with baseline scheduler vs prototype knobs and send a results summary.
Follow-up call to review benchmark results and decide whether to proceed with a Dedicated pilot (short canary pool) or keep evaluation on Hosted.
action_items: Claire Dubois - Email benchmark harness details + scenario definitions + metrics checklist - due 2025-11-21
Arjun Mehta - Provide anonymized length distribution + concurrency/burst stats (no prompt content) - due 2025-11-21
Lena Fischer - Propose initial short/long threshold candidates and default guardrails (aging, token budgets) based on Northpeak stats - due 2025-11-25
Sean Gallagher - Share SLO guardrail recommendations for canary (rollback triggers for p95 drift) - due 2025-11-25

Meeting header
Date: 2025-11-19
Time: 08:00 PT / 11:00 ET
Duration: 53 minutes
Call type: Technical deep dive

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Lena Fischer, Claire Dubois, Sean Gallagher
Northpeak AI: Arjun Mehta, Sarah Nguyen, Priya Desai, Jason Liu

Auto-summary (Fireflies)

- Reviewed prefill vs decode contention and continuous batching behavior.
- Redwood described a short/long aware scheduler prototype to reduce p95.
- Agreed to run benchmarks and share anonymized distribution stats.

Topics

2) Where p95 is coming from (queue vs prefill vs decode)

Transcript

[00:00] Lena Fischer: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for making time. This one’s meant to be a deeper dive on the tail latency you’ve been seeing when you have like short chat traffic mixed with long-context traffic. I’m Lena, I’m on the serving runtime side, scheduling.

[00:14] Arjun Mehta: Hey, yep. I’m Arjun, I run platform. Sarah’s on ML infra. Priya is here for, like, security constraints. Jason on applied.

[00:22] Sarah Nguyen: Hi.

[00:23] Priya Desai: Hi.

[00:24] Jason Liu: Hey.

[00:26] Lena Fischer: Great. Claire is here too, she owns a lot of our benchmark methodology and trace replay. Sean is SRE, mostly to sanity check what we’d consider safe guardrails if we do any canary later.

[00:38] Sean Gallagher: Hey all.

[00:39] Claire Dubois: Hi.

[00:41] Lena Fischer: Maybe we start with you all describing the symptoms, but specifically: is it time-to-first-token that’s spiking, or like end-to-end for the whole response? And what your SLO is.

[00:55] Arjun Mehta: Yeah, it’s mostly TTFT and p95. So we do chat. Most users expect like sub-second first token. Our internal goal is p95 TTFT under 800 milliseconds, and p99 under 1.5 seconds. When we get long-context traffic, we see p95 TTFT jump to like 1.4, 1.6 seconds. It’s super noticeable.

[01:19] Sarah Nguyen: And end-to-end also moves, but customers complain about that first token delay first.

[01:24] Lena Fischer: Got it. And those long-context requests, what are we talking, like 8k? 32k? 100k?

[01:32] Jason Liu: Mixed. We have a RAG pipeline. Typical context is 6k to 12k input tokens. The long tail is like 40k-ish. We do have a couple workflows that push bigger but… those are less common.

[01:46] Lena Fischer: Okay. And concurrency? Like steady QPS and burst shape.

[01:50] Arjun Mehta: Steady is 60 to 120 RPS depending on time of day. Bursts can go 3x for a minute.

[01:58] Sarah Nguyen: Also we have some batch-ish jobs that call the same endpoint. It’s not fully separated, which is partly why we’re here.

[02:06] Lena Fischer: Yep, that’s basically the classic “mixed workloads break continuous batching assumptions” thing.

[02:11] Priya Desai: Just to flag, we can share distribution stats, but we can’t share prompt content. Even tokenized content is risky for us.

[02:18] Lena Fischer: Totally. We don’t need content. Bucket counts and lengths are enough.

[02:22] Claire Dubois: Yeah, we typically ask for something like: histogram of input tokens, output tokens, maybe p50/p95 per route, and concurrency over time.

[02:31] Arjun Mehta: We can do that.

[02:33] Lena Fischer: Cool. So let me reflect what we think is happening, then you can tell me if it matches what you’re seeing.

[02:39] Lena Fischer: In a continuous batching system, when a long-context request hits, its prefill step can be heavy. If your scheduler is mostly “take whatever is at the front of the queue” and build a batch, long-prefill can dominate the GPU for some window. Meanwhile short chat prompts are waiting behind it, so their queue time balloons, and TTFT looks bad. Even if average throughput is fine.

[03:03] Sarah Nguyen: That sounds like it, yeah.

[03:05] Jason Liu: We also see weird behavior where the GPU utilization looks high but latency is still bad. Like it’s doing work but not the work the users care about.

[03:12] Lena Fischer: Exactly. It can be “efficient” but not “user-optimal”.

[03:15] Sean Gallagher: And from SRE perspective it shows up as p95 drift even if error rate is stable.

[03:20] Arjun Mehta: Yup.

[03:22] Lena Fischer: Can I ask what you’re currently running? Self-hosted vLLM? Triton? Or managed endpoints?

[03:28] Arjun Mehta: Today we have a mix. Some workloads are on AWS Bedrock, some we self-host with vLLM on EKS. We’re evaluating a move to a dedicated provider because we don’t want to keep rebuilding this. We’ve looked at Together, Anyscale. You guys came up because of tail latency claims.

[03:46] Lena Fischer: Makes sense.

[03:47] Sarah Nguyen: With vLLM we tried to tune max batch tokens and stuff, but it’s always a trade: either long requests tank everyone else or you make batching conservative and cost goes up.

[03:58] Lena Fischer: Yep. That’s basically the trade. What we’re prototyping internally is a policy that’s aware of “short vs long” at the scheduler level. Two queues, essentially.

[04:08] Arjun Mehta: Like priority queueing?

[04:10] Lena Fischer: Kind of. Not strict priority, because then long can starve. It’s more class-based scheduling with guardrails.

[04:17] Lena Fischer: The prototype approach:
- We classify each request at enqueue time (short or long) based on input tokens, and optionally a predicted prefill cost.
- We maintain separate queues.
- Dispatch picks from the short queue more aggressively to protect TTFT, but we enforce aging so long requests get service even under sustained short traffic.
- We also put per-iteration token budgets, so one class can’t consume the full GPU step repeatedly.

[04:47] Jason Liu: When you say “iteration”, you mean a scheduling tick that forms a batch for decode?

[04:52] Lena Fischer: Yep. Think of a step where we decide what goes into the next GPU launch, both for prefill and decode. Implementation detail varies, but that’s the idea.

[05:01] Sarah Nguyen: Do you separate prefill and decode explicitly?

[05:04] Lena Fischer: We’re adding hooks for that. One of the failure modes in mixed workloads is prefill and decode competing in the same selection logic. So we’re adding a separation so long-prefill can’t dominate decode selection, and vice versa.

[05:19] Arjun Mehta: Okay.

[05:20] Lena Fischer: Practically for you, what it means is: short chat requests should see lower time-in-queue and faster TTFT, especially p95, under mixes like 80/20 short/long. Long requests might get slightly slower TTFT, but they should still make progress and not starve.

[05:40] Arjun Mehta: What’s the typical improvement you see?

[05:43] Lena Fischer: Depends on model and mix. In synthetic 80/20 we’ve seen p95 TTFT for short class drop like 25-40% compared to baseline scheduler, with throughput within ~0-5% if knobs are tuned. But I don’t want to oversell without running your distribution.

[06:02] Claire Dubois: The improvements are most dramatic when the “long” is truly long prefill and arrives in bursts. If everything is moderately long, there’s less to prioritize.

[06:12] Jason Liu: That tracks.

[06:14] Priya Desai: And this is available where? Hosted only, or can we do it in a VPC deployment.

[06:20] Lena Fischer: This prototype is in our runtime. So it can apply in Hosted, Dedicated, and Private, as long as you’re on the runtime version that includes it and we enable the feature flag. For a first evaluation, we’d probably do it on a Dedicated pool so we can control config and get clean metrics, but we can start with Hosted if that’s simpler.

[06:40] Arjun Mehta: We likely need Dedicated at minimum, maybe VPC, because of data policy.

[06:45] Priya Desai: Yes. We prefer VPC or at least strong isolation and retention controls. Also SSO, audit logs, KMS integration, you know the list.

[06:53] Sean Gallagher: Understood. For today, we can keep it to performance. But yes, Dedicated gives you isolation; Private gives you VPC/on-prem style. We can follow up with security review if this goes well.

[07:06] Lena Fischer: Back to performance: can you describe your “short” requests? Like typical input tokens and output tokens.

[07:12] Sarah Nguyen: Short is like 200-800 input tokens. Output maybe 100-300 tokens.

[07:18] Jason Liu: Some are smaller, like 80 tokens input. But that’s the median-ish.

[07:24] Lena Fischer: And long requests: you said 6k-12k typical, up to 40k. Output similar?

[07:30] Jason Liu: Output might be similar, but sometimes bigger because it’s summarization.

[07:34] Lena Fischer: Okay.

[07:36] Claire Dubois: So classification threshold might be around, I don’t know, 2k or 3k input tokens, but we can tune. We also do predicted prefill time, but that’s more complex.

[07:46] Arjun Mehta: How do you prevent gaming? Like if a customer sends something slightly below threshold.

[07:51] Lena Fischer: In the prototype this is internal knobs, not customer-facing tiers. Long term you’d want something more robust, like token-based fairness. But for now, in a dedicated pool, you can just pick a threshold that matches your distribution.

[08:05] Arjun Mehta: Makes sense.

[08:07] Sarah Nguyen: What about fairness? We have some enterprise workflows where a long doc summary can’t just hang for minutes.

[08:14] Lena Fischer: Yeah. That’s why we do aging. Concretely: each request’s priority increases as it waits. So even if short queue is busy, long queue items eventually get promoted in effect. We also cap “max skew” so you can’t do 99% short forever.

[08:32] Sean Gallagher: And we track starvation counters. If those trip, we treat it as a rollback signal in canary.

[08:38] Priya Desai: Rollback as in, you can disable it quickly.

[08:41] Sean Gallagher: Feature flag, yes.

[08:43] Lena Fischer: Exactly.

[08:44] Jason Liu: One other thing we saw: sometimes kernels look unstable, like it’s switching between paths and causing jitter. Does mixing lengths cause that?

[08:54] Lena Fischer: It can. When sequence length distributions change rapidly, kernel selection can thrash, especially around prefill vs decode shapes. Part of our work here is to make sure the scheduling doesn’t induce shape oscillation. We’ve added some guardrails around token budgeting and grouping.

[09:11] Sarah Nguyen: Okay. So you’d want to keep batches more homogeneous?

[09:14] Lena Fischer: Right, without killing utilization. That’s the balance.

[09:19] Arjun Mehta: What are the metrics you’d want us to look at in the benchmark?

[09:23] Claire Dubois: Minimum set:
- TTFT p50/p95/p99
- End-to-end latency p50/p95/p99
- Queue time (time-in-queue) broken out, if possible
- Prefill latency vs decode latency
- Throughput (tokens/sec) and cost proxy (GPU-hours per million tokens)
- And then per-class versions of those if we enable the two-queue policy

[09:50] Lena Fischer: Also error rate and any timeouts.

[09:53] Arjun Mehta: And success criteria, we should define.

[09:56] Lena Fischer: Yes. What would you consider a win?

[10:00] Arjun Mehta: For short chat traffic, under mixed workload, if we can get p95 TTFT back under 900ms consistently, and keep throughput within 10% of current. Ideally within 5%.

[10:14] Sarah Nguyen: And not destroy long requests. Like long p95 can go up a bit but not like double.

[10:19] Jason Liu: Maybe “long class p95 TTFT increases less than 20%” or “max wait < X seconds”. We can define.

[10:28] Sean Gallagher: That’s a good way to state it. Max wait or bounded slowdown.

[10:33] Priya Desai: Also we need predictable behavior. If it improves p95 but introduces occasional huge spikes, that’s not good.

[10:40] Lena Fischer: Yep, so we’ll look at p99 too.

[10:43] (crosstalk)

[10:44] Lena Fischer: Sorry, go ahead.

[10:45] Priya Desai: And operationally, we need transparency. Like can we see dashboards per class.

[10:51] Sean Gallagher: Yes, we have per-class queue depth, waiting time, dispatch share. If we do a dedicated pilot, we’d share a dashboard view.

[11:01] Arjun Mehta: Okay.

[11:03] Lena Fischer: Let’s talk about the benchmark we propose. We have a standard set: 80/20 short/long, 50/50, and a “long spike” where you inject a burst of long-prefill for 2 minutes while short continues. That last one is usually what breaks systems.

[11:22] Sarah Nguyen: That’s exactly what we see in production. Our batch jobs kick off and then support gets yelled at.

[11:28] Lena Fischer: Yep.

[11:29] Claire Dubois: If you can provide just the histogram and typical output lengths, we can synthesize prompts with the same lengths but no content. Or you can provide token counts only, and we generate dummy tokens.

[11:41] Priya Desai: Dummy tokens is fine.

[11:43] Arjun Mehta: We can send length stats.

[11:46] Lena Fischer: Great.

[11:47] Jason Liu: Are you running this on which models? We’re on a 70B-ish class.

[11:53] Lena Fischer: We can do it on the closest match in our catalog. If you’re evaluating a specific open model, we can run that. For the scheduling effect, model architecture matters but the phenomenon is similar.

[12:07] Sarah Nguyen: Our current is Llama 3.1 70B-ish and some fine-tune.

[12:12] Lena Fischer: Okay, we can use a comparable 70B base. Fine-tune specifics aren’t needed for scheduler behavior.

[12:20] Arjun Mehta: Hardware matters too. We’re mostly A100 right now.

[12:24] Claire Dubois: We’ll run at least A100 80GB, and we can also run H100 to show the shape.

[12:31] Arjun Mehta: Okay.

[12:33] Lena Fischer: Let’s do a quick dig into where your p95 is coming from. Do you have a breakdown today? Like queue time vs compute time.

[12:41] Sarah Nguyen: We have some traces. Not perfect. It looks like queue time jumps when long prompts are active. TTFT roughly tracks queue time.

[12:50] Lena Fischer: That’s consistent.

[12:52] Jason Liu: Also KV cache behavior. Sometimes after a long request, the next ones are weirdly slower.

[12:59] Lena Fischer: That could be cache eviction or compaction overhead. Mixing long contexts can thrash KV. Our prototype doesn’t “solve” KV memory limits, but by isolating long requests you can reduce how often they collide in the same batch. Also we have some compaction tuning, but that’s separate.

[13:18] Arjun Mehta: Right.

[13:20] Priya Desai: I know it’s not today’s focus, but if we do Dedicated, we need to know data handling. Is any prompt stored.

[13:28] Sean Gallagher: Generally we don’t store prompts by default; logs can be configured; metrics are aggregated. For a pilot we can align on retention. We can do a separate security review.

[13:40] Priya Desai: Okay.

[13:42] Lena Fischer: Back to scheduling knobs. For the prototype, there are a few relevant parameters:
- short_long_threshold_tokens (input)
- short_queue_share_target (like 0.7)
- aging_half_life_seconds (how fast long gets promoted)
- per_iteration_token_budget_short/long
- burst_cap_short (so short doesn’t dominate)

[14:06] Arjun Mehta: Those are adjustable per pool.

[14:08] Lena Fischer: Yes.

[14:10] Jason Liu: How do you choose the threshold? Just by histogram.

[14:13] Lena Fischer: Start with the valley between modes. If you have a bimodal distribution, it’s easy. If it’s continuous, then we pick a pragmatic cutoff that protects “most chats” and treat the rest as long. Then we validate by running the scenarios.

[14:28] Claire Dubois: We can also do a sensitivity sweep: threshold at 1k, 2k, 4k and see where p95 improves without too much long pain.

[14:37] Sarah Nguyen: That’d be great.

[14:39] Arjun Mehta: What are the risks? Like could it make throughput worse.

[14:43] Lena Fischer: Risks:
1) Throughput regression if we over-segment and lose batching efficiency.
2) Long starvation if aging is misconfigured.
3) Kernel selection instability if we bounce shapes too hard.
4) If your workload isn’t actually “mixed lengths” but “mixed output lengths”, then this won’t help as much.

[15:07] Arjun Mehta: Understood.

[15:09] Sean Gallagher: Operationally, during canary we’d watch p95/p99 drift, plus starvation counters, plus queue depth. If any trip, rollback.

[15:19] Priya Desai: Okay.

[15:21] Lena Fischer: So what I propose is: we do an offline benchmark first. No production changes. Just run scenarios on our side.

[15:29] Arjun Mehta: Yeah.

[15:30] Lena Fischer: Claire will send you what we need for the synthetic generator. You send histogram + output lengths + concurrency profile. Then we run baseline scheduler vs prototype scheduler with a small parameter sweep.

[15:44] Claire Dubois: And we’ll include the “long spike” scenario, because that’s typically the deciding one.

[15:50] Arjun Mehta: Great.

[15:52] Jason Liu: Can we also test a scenario where long requests are like 10% but arrive in a burst, which is what our batch job does.

[16:00] Claire Dubois: Yes, that’s basically long-spike.

[16:03] Sarah Nguyen: Cool.

[16:05] Lena Fischer: If the results look good, then next step would be a small Dedicated pilot. Probably a canary pool in one region, with guardrails. But we don’t need to decide today.

[16:17] Arjun Mehta: What’s your typical timeline from benchmark to pilot.

[16:21] Lena Fischer: If we get inputs by Friday, we can usually run this early next week. Then a review meeting. If you want a pilot, depends on procurement, but technically we can stand up Dedicated quickly.

[16:34] Priya Desai: For procurement we’d need a security review, SOC2, pen test docs, SSO. That’s usually 2-3 weeks.

[16:43] Sean Gallagher: Yep, we can start that in parallel if you want.

[16:47] Arjun Mehta: Let’s see the performance first.

[16:49] Lena Fischer: Sounds good.

[16:50] (pause)

[16:52] Sarah Nguyen: One more question: how does this compare to just doing strict SRPT. Like shortest remaining processing time.

[16:58] Lena Fischer: SRPT is great for mean response time but it’s tricky in practice because “remaining processing” changes during decode, and you can starve long. Also you need good prediction. Our two-queue is like a simpler SRPT approximation with explicit guardrails.

[17:15] Jason Liu: Makes sense.

[17:17] Arjun Mehta: And compared to admission control. Like just reject long jobs.

[17:21] Lena Fischer: That works but you’re basically pushing the problem to the user. Also you said you need those long workflows to complete. So scheduling is the right lever.

[17:31] Arjun Mehta: Agreed.

[17:33] Priya Desai: Are there any user-visible changes. Like would responses be different.

[17:38] Lena Fischer: No change in model output. It’s purely scheduling.

[17:43] Priya Desai: Good.

[17:44] Lena Fischer: Okay, I think we’re aligned. Before we wrap, let’s confirm next steps:
- Claire sends benchmark checklist and scenarios.
- Arjun/Sarah send histograms + concurrency.
- We run baseline vs prototype on A100 and H100 and send results.
- Schedule follow-up to review.

[18:06] Arjun Mehta: Yes.

[18:07] Sarah Nguyen: Yep.

[18:08] Priya Desai: Okay.

[18:10] Sean Gallagher: Works.

[18:12] Lena Fischer: Great. Thanks everyone. We’ll follow up over email.

[18:18] (Meeting ended)
